name: Napoleonic Wars
summary: Napoleon's French Empire and its satellites fought a series of coalitions financed by Britain and fielded mainly by Austria, Russia and Prussia. Napoleon dominated the continent after Austerlitz, Jena and Friedland, but the Peninsular War and the disaster in Russia in 1812 broke his power, and he was defeated at Leipzig, forced to abdicate in 1814 and finally beaten at Waterloo in 1815. The wars spread French law and administration, awakened nationalism and left Britain the leading world power after the Congress of Vienna.

steps.title: War of the Third Coalition
steps.text: Britain had been at war with France again since 1803, and Napoleon, crowned emperor in 1804, gathered an invasion army at Boulogne. When Austria and Russia joined Britain he marched the Grande Armee to the Danube, trapped Mack's Austrians at Ulm and took Vienna, while Nelson destroyed the Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar. At Austerlitz Napoleon routed the Russian and Austrian armies, and Austria made peace at Pressburg.

moves.label: Russian army falls back to Olmutz

events.name: Ulm
events.text: Napoleon encircled Mack's army, which surrendered with about 25,000 men.

events.name: Battle of Trafalgar
events.text: Nelson destroyed the Franco-Spanish fleet and died in the battle, ending any French hope of invading Britain.

events.name: Battle of Austerlitz
events.text: Napoleon broke the allied centre on the Pratzen Heights in his most celebrated victory.

steps.label: 1806 to 1807
steps.title: War of the Fourth Coalition
steps.text: Napoleon replaced the Holy Roman Empire with his Confederation of the Rhine, and Prussia went to war. In one day at Jena and Auerstedt the Prussian army was destroyed and Napoleon entered Berlin, then pushed into Poland against the Russians. After a bloody draw at Eylau he won at Friedland, and the Treaties of Tilsit made Tsar Alexander his ally.

moves.label: Through Thuringia to Berlin and Poland

events.name: Battle of Jena-Auerstedt
events.text: Twin French victories destroyed the Prussian army in a single day.

events.name: Battle of Friedland
events.text: Napoleon routed Bennigsen's Russians and forced the Tsar to seek peace.

events.name: Treaties of Tilsit
events.text: Russia became France's ally and Prussia lost half its territory.

steps.title: The Peninsular War begins
steps.text: Napoleon occupied Portugal, then deposed the Spanish Bourbons and made his brother Joseph king of Spain, setting off a national uprising. A Spanish army forced a French corps to surrender at Bailen and Wellesley's British army freed Portugal, so Napoleon came in person, retook Madrid and chased Sir John Moore's army to Corunna. The war in Iberia became a running sore that drained French strength for six years.

fronts.label: French fall back to the Ebro, Aug 1808

moves.label: Moore's advance and retreat to Corunna

events.name: Battle of Bailen
events.text: Castanos forced Dupont's corps to surrender, the first defeat of a Napoleonic army in the field.

events.name: Napoleon enters Madrid
events.text: Napoleon smashed the Spanish armies and reinstalled Joseph in the capital.

events.name: Battle of Corunna
events.text: Moore held off Soult so his army could escape by sea, but was killed.

steps.title: War of the Fifth Coalition
steps.text: With Napoleon's best troops in Spain, Austria struck again. Napoleon beat Archduke Charles in Bavaria and took Vienna, but his attempt to cross the Danube was thrown back at Aspern-Essling, his first personal defeat. Six weeks later he crossed in force and won the huge battle of Wagram, and Austria made peace and gave Napoleon an archduchess as wife, while Wellesley won at Talavera in Spain.

moves.label: Austrian invasion of Bavaria and retreat to the Marchfeld
Napoleon to Vienna and across the Danube

events.name: Battle of Aspern-Essling
events.text: Archduke Charles threw Napoleon back across the Danube.

events.name: Battle of Wagram
events.text: Napoleon won a two-day battle of over 300,000 men and forced Austria to make peace.

events.name: Battle of Talavera
events.text: Wellesley repulsed the French and was made Viscount Wellington.

steps.label: 1810 to 1812
steps.title: Invasion of Russia
steps.text: In Iberia Wellington held Massena at the Lines of Torres Vedras in 1810 and won at Salamanca in 1812. Meanwhile Russia broke with the Continental System, and Napoleon crossed the Niemen with over 600,000 men. The Russians retreated, fought at Borodino and abandoned Moscow, which burned; when the Tsar would not negotiate, the Grande Armee retreated through the winter and was almost destroyed.

events.name: Battle of Salamanca
events.text: Wellington routed Marmont's army in a swift flank attack.

events.name: Battle of Borodino
events.text: The bloodiest day of the wars left Napoleon the field and the road to Moscow, but not a decisive victory.

events.name: Crossing of the Berezina
events.text: Napoleon escaped across the river on improvised bridges but lost tens of thousands.

steps.title: War of the Sixth Coalition
steps.text: Prussia and then Austria and Sweden joined Russia and Britain. Napoleon rebuilt an army and won at Lutzen, Bautzen and Dresden, but three allied armies closed on him at Leipzig, where the Battle of the Nations drove him out of Germany. In Spain Wellington broke Joseph's army at Vitoria and pushed the French back to the Pyrenees.

events.name: Battle of Vitoria
events.text: Wellington broke Joseph Bonaparte's army and ended French rule in Spain.

events.name: Battle of Dresden
events.text: Napoleon's last great victory in Germany drove back the Army of Bohemia.

events.name: Battle of Leipzig
events.text: The Battle of the Nations, the largest battle in Europe before 1914, drove Napoleon out of Germany.

steps.title: The fall of Paris
steps.text: The allies invaded France from the east while Wellington crossed the Pyrenees in the south. Napoleon won a string of brilliant victories in the Six Days' Campaign but could not stop the converging armies, and Paris fell on 31 March. His marshals refused to fight on, and he abdicated at Fontainebleau and was exiled to Elba as the Bourbons returned.

moves.label: Army of Silesia across the Rhine
Napoleon strikes between the allied armies

events.name: Six Days' Campaign
events.text: Napoleon beat Blucher's scattered corps at Champaubert, Montmirail and Vauchamps.

events.name: Battle of Paris
events.text: The allies stormed the heights around Paris and the city capitulated.

events.name: Abdication at Fontainebleau
events.text: Napoleon gave up his throne and was sent to Elba.

steps.label: Mar to Jun 1815
steps.title: The Hundred Days and Waterloo
steps.text: Napoleon escaped from Elba and marched on Paris as the army rallied to him, while Murat in Naples rose in his support and was crushed. He struck into Belgium and beat the Prussians at Ligny, but at Waterloo Wellington's army held until Blucher arrived, and the French army collapsed. Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena and the Congress of Vienna redrew the map of Europe.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Battle of Ligny
events.text: Napoleon defeated Blucher, but the Prussian army withdrew intact.

events.name: Battle of Waterloo
events.text: Wellington's army held until the Prussians arrived, and Napoleon's army broke.

events.name: Congress of Vienna
events.text: The victors restored monarchies and set a balance of power that lasted decades.

name: Serbian Revolution and Greek War of Independence
summary: Between 1804 and 1830 Serbs and then Greeks rose against Ottoman rule in the first national revolutions of the Balkans. Serbia won autonomy after two uprisings, and the Greek revolt, near defeat after Egypt intervened, was saved when Britain, France and Russia destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino and Russia beat the Ottomans in 1828 to 1829. Autonomous Serbia and an independent Greece began the long break-up of Ottoman Europe.

steps.label: 1804 to 1806
steps.title: The First Serbian Uprising
steps.text: In the Pashalik of Belgrade, renegade janissaries murdered Serbian notables, and in 1804 the Serbs rose under the livestock trader Karadjordje. A revolt against local tyrants became a war against the Sultan: the rebels beat Ottoman armies at Ivankovac and Misar and took Belgrade. When Russia went to war with the Ottomans in 1806 it backed the Serbs.

events.name: Orasac assembly
events.text: Serbian leaders chose Karadjordje to lead the uprising.

events.name: Battle of Ivankovac
events.text: The first rebel victory over a regular Ottoman army turned the revolt into a war with the Sultan.

events.name: Battle of Misar
events.text: Karadjordje defeated the Bosnian army, and Belgrade fell to the rebels that winter.

steps.label: 1809 to 1817
steps.title: Defeat and the Second Uprising
steps.text: Napoleon's invasion pulled Russia out of the war in 1812, and in 1813 Ottoman armies converged on Serbia from three sides, retook Belgrade and drove Karadjordje into exile. In 1815 Milos Obrenovic raised a second uprising at Takovo and won a negotiated autonomy, becoming prince of Serbia. Karadjordje returned in 1817 and was murdered on Milos's orders.

events.name: Battle of Cegar
events.text: Stevan Sindjelic blew up his own redoubt; the Ottomans built the Skull Tower from the dead.

events.name: Fall of Belgrade
events.text: The Ottoman reconquest ended the first uprising and Karadjordje fled to Austria.

events.name: Takovo uprising
events.text: Milos Obrenovic launched the second revolt, which won Serbian autonomy.

steps.label: 1821 to 1822
steps.title: The Greek Revolution
steps.text: The secret Filiki Eteria launched the revolt: Ypsilantis crossed into Moldavia but was crushed at Dragasani, while the Peloponnese rose in March 1821. Kolokotronis took Tripolitsa, the Greek fleet ruled the Aegean, and Dramali Pasha's great army was destroyed in the passes at Dervenakia. The Ottomans massacred the islanders of Chios, a crime that turned European opinion toward the Greeks.

moves.label: Sacred Band in the Danubian Principalities

events.name: Siege of Tripolitsa
events.text: Kolokotronis stormed the Ottoman capital of the Morea, followed by a massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

events.name: Chios massacre
events.text: Ottoman troops killed or enslaved most of the island's Greek population.

events.name: Battle of Dervenakia
events.text: Kolokotronis trapped and destroyed Dramali's army in the mountain passes.

steps.label: 1825 to 1827
steps.title: Ibrahim Pasha and Missolonghi
steps.text: Divided by civil war, the Greeks faced a new enemy when the Sultan called in Muhammad Ali of Egypt. His son Ibrahim Pasha landed a modern army in the Morea in 1825 and laid waste to it, while Resid Mehmed Pasha besieged Missolonghi, which fell after a desperate breakout in April 1826. By 1827 Athens had fallen too and the revolt seemed lost.

events.name: Ibrahim lands at Methoni
events.text: Egyptian regulars arrived and began reconquering the Peloponnese.

events.name: Fall of Missolonghi
events.text: After a year-long siege the starving defenders broke out and most were killed.

events.name: Fall of the Acropolis
events.text: Resid Mehmed took Athens, the last Greek stronghold north of the Gulf of Corinth.

steps.label: 1827 to 1828
steps.title: Navarino
steps.text: Britain, France and Russia agreed in the Treaty of London to impose an armistice and sent their fleets to Greece. At Navarino Bay their ships under Codrington destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet in an afternoon, cutting Ibrahim off from Egypt. A French expedition under Maison landed in the Morea in 1828 and Ibrahim's army sailed home.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Battle of Navarino
events.text: The allied fleets sank most of the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet, the last great battle of sailing ships.

events.name: Morea expedition
events.text: French troops landed at Petalidi and oversaw the departure of the Egyptian army.

steps.label: 1828 to 1830
steps.title: Russia forces the peace
steps.text: Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire in 1828. Diebitsch beat the Grand Vizier at Kulevcha, crossed the Balkan mountains and took Adrianople within striking distance of Constantinople. The Treaty of Adrianople confirmed Serbian autonomy and Greek self-rule, and in 1830 the London Protocol recognised Greece as an independent kingdom while Milos became hereditary prince of Serbia.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: Russian army over the Balkan mountains

events.name: Battle of Kulevcha
events.text: Diebitsch routed the Grand Vizier and opened the road over the mountains.

events.name: Treaty of Adrianople
events.text: The Sultan accepted Serbian autonomy and Greek self-government under Russian pressure.

name: Spanish American wars of independence
summary: When Napoleon seized Spain in 1808, juntas across Spanish America took power in the king's name, and the revolts of 1810 grew into wars for independence. After royalist armies crushed the first republics, Jose de San Martin crossed the Andes to free Chile, Simon Bolivar crossed them to free New Granada and Venezuela, Mexico broke away in 1821, and the last royalist army in Peru surrendered at Ayacucho in 1824. Spain lost all its mainland American empire, which split into new republics.

steps.label: 1808 to 1811
steps.title: The revolutions of 1810
steps.text: Napoleon's capture of King Ferdinand VII in 1808 left Spanish America without a legitimate ruler, and in 1810 juntas took power in Caracas, Buenos Aires, Bogota and Santiago. In Mexico the priest Miguel Hidalgo called the people to arms at Dolores and led a vast peasant army to the gates of Mexico City before Calleja destroyed it at Calderon Bridge. Buenos Aires sent an army north into Upper Peru, but it was beaten at Huaqui.

polities: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

moves.label: Army of the North into Upper Peru

events.name: Grito de Dolores
events.text: Hidalgo's call to revolt began the Mexican War of Independence.

events.name: May Revolution
events.text: A junta in Buenos Aires deposed the Spanish viceroy.

events.name: Battle of Calderon Bridge
events.text: Calleja routed Hidalgo's army; Hidalgo was captured and executed.

steps.label: 1812 to 1816
steps.title: The royalist reconquest
steps.text: The first republics fell one by one. Bolivar's Admirable Campaign retook Caracas in 1813, but royalist llaneros under Boves destroyed his Second Republic, Chile's patriots were crushed at Rancagua, and Morelos was executed in Mexico. In 1815 Spain sent Morillo with 10,000 veterans, who took Cartagena and reconquered New Granada, leaving only the Rio de la Plata free, where independence was declared at Tucuman in 1816.

polities: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

moves.label: Royalist expedition from Peru to Chile

events.name: Battle of Rancagua
events.text: Osorio defeated O'Higgins and ended Chile's first republic.

events.name: Siege of Cartagena
events.text: Morillo starved the port into surrender and reconquered New Granada.

events.name: Congress of Tucuman
events.text: The United Provinces of South America declared independence from Spain.

steps.label: 1817 to 1818
steps.title: San Martin crosses the Andes
steps.text: San Martin trained the Army of the Andes at Mendoza and in January 1817 led it over passes nearly 4,000 metres high. With O'Higgins he won at Chacabuco and entered Santiago, and after a setback at Cancha Rayada he destroyed Osorio's army at Maipu, securing Chile's independence. Guemes's gaucho guerrillas meanwhile held the royalists back on the northern frontier.

polities: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fronts.label: Salta and Jujuy frontier, held by Guemes

events.name: Battle of Chacabuco
events.text: The Army of the Andes beat the royalists and opened the road to Santiago.

events.name: Battle of Maipu
events.text: San Martin destroyed Osorio's army and sealed Chilean independence.

steps.title: Bolivar crosses the Andes
steps.text: With Morillo holding northern Venezuela, Bolivar struck where he was not expected. In the rainy season he led his army from the llanos over the frozen Paramo de Pisba into New Granada, beat the royalists at Boyaca and marched into Bogota. The Congress of Angostura then proclaimed the Republic of Colombia, uniting Venezuela and New Granada.

polities: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

moves.label: Bolivar over the Andes to Bogota

events.name: Battle of Boyaca
events.text: Bolivar captured most of Barreiro's army and freed New Granada.

events.name: Gran Colombia proclaimed
events.text: The Congress of Angostura united Venezuela and New Granada as one republic.

steps.label: 1821 to 1822
steps.title: Carabobo, Lima and Mexico
steps.text: A liberal revolt in Spain in 1820 stopped reinforcements. Bolivar destroyed the royalist army of Venezuela at Carabobo, San Martin sailed from Chile with Cochrane's fleet and entered Lima, and Sucre freed Quito at Pichincha. In Mexico the royalist officer Iturbide changed sides, and the Treaty of Cordoba recognised Mexican independence in 1821.

polities: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

moves.label: Liberating Expedition of Peru with Cochrane's fleet

events.name: Battle of Carabobo
events.text: Bolivar's victory decided the independence of Venezuela.

events.name: Treaty of Cordoba
events.text: The last Spanish viceroy accepted Mexican independence.

events.name: Battle of Pichincha
events.text: Sucre won on the slopes of the volcano above Quito and freed Ecuador.

steps.label: 1823 to 1826
steps.title: Junin and Ayacucho
steps.text: San Martin withdrew after meeting Bolivar at Guayaquil, and the royalists still held highland Peru under Viceroy La Serna. Bolivar and Sucre marched over the Andes and won the cavalry battle of Junin, and on 9 December 1824 Sucre destroyed the last royalist army at Ayacucho, capturing the viceroy. Upper Peru became Bolivia, and the last Spanish garrison at Callao surrendered in January 1826.

polities: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

moves.label: United Liberating Army over the Andes

events.name: Battle of Junin
events.text: Patriot cavalry routed Canterac's horsemen in a fight fought entirely with lances and sabres.

events.name: Battle of Ayacucho
events.text: Sucre destroyed the last royalist army and captured Viceroy La Serna.

events.name: Surrender of Callao
events.text: The last Spanish stronghold on the South American mainland gave up after a long siege.

name: War of 1812
summary: The United States declared war on Britain in 1812 over the seizure of American sailors, trade restrictions and British support for Native resistance in the Northwest, hoping to conquer Canada. American invasions of Canada failed, British raids burned Washington but were repulsed at Baltimore and Plattsburgh, and the Treaty of Ghent restored the prewar borders. The war secured Canada for Britain, boosted American nationalism and destroyed Tecumseh's Native confederacy.

steps.title: The invasion of Canada fails
steps.text: Expecting Canada to fall easily, the United States attacked across the border. Instead General Hull, outmanoeuvred by Isaac Brock and Tecumseh, surrendered Detroit without a fight, and an American crossing of the Niagara was beaten at Queenston Heights, where Brock was killed. At sea the frigate USS Constitution gave the Americans a morale-lifting victory over HMS Guerriere.

events.name: Surrender of Detroit
events.text: Hull surrendered his army and Michigan to a smaller British and Native force.

events.name: USS Constitution vs HMS Guerriere
events.text: The American frigate shattered a British warship and earned the name Old Ironsides.

events.name: Battle of Queenston Heights
events.text: The Niagara invasion was thrown back, but Brock was killed.

steps.title: The Great Lakes
steps.text: Both sides raced to build fleets on the lakes. Americans raided York, the capital of Upper Canada, and Oliver Hazard Perry won control of Lake Erie, forcing the British to abandon Detroit. Harrison caught the retreating British and Native army at the Thames, where Tecumseh was killed, but an American drive on Montreal failed at Crysler's Farm.

moves.label: Drive down the St Lawrence on Montreal

events.name: Battle of Lake Erie
events.text: Perry captured the whole British squadron: we have met the enemy and they are ours.

events.name: Battle of the Thames
events.text: Tecumseh's death broke the Native confederacy.

events.name: Battle of Crysler's Farm
events.text: A small British force turned back the American advance on Montreal.

steps.title: Britain strikes back
steps.text: With Napoleon defeated, Britain sent veteran troops across the Atlantic. On the Niagara the Americans fought well at Chippawa and Lundy's Lane, but in August a British force under Ross and Cochrane routed militia at Bladensburg and burned Washington. The tide turned in September: Baltimore's Fort McHenry withstood bombardment, and Macdonough's naval victory at Plattsburgh sent Prevost's invasion army back to Canada.

moves.label: British fleet up the Chesapeake to Baltimore

events.name: Burning of Washington
events.text: British troops burned the Capitol and the White House.

events.name: Battle of Plattsburgh
events.text: Macdonough destroyed the British lake squadron and Prevost retreated.

events.name: Battle of Baltimore
events.text: Fort McHenry held through the night, inspiring The Star-Spangled Banner.

steps.label: Dec 1814 to Jan 1815
steps.title: Ghent and New Orleans
steps.text: Negotiators at Ghent signed a peace on Christmas Eve 1814 that restored the prewar borders. News travelled slowly, and a British army under Pakenham attacked New Orleans in January 1815, only to be shattered by Andrew Jackson's entrenched mixed force. The victory made Jackson a national hero and let Americans remember the war as a triumph.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: Jackson from Mobile to New Orleans

events.name: Treaty of Ghent
events.text: The peace restored all conquests and settled none of the original grievances.

events.name: Battle of New Orleans
events.text: Jackson's defenders inflicted about 2,000 casualties and killed Pakenham.

name: Opium Wars
summary: Two wars in which Britain, joined by France in the second, used naval and military power to force Qing China to accept the opium trade and open to Western commerce. The First Opium War (1839 to 1842) ended with the Treaty of Nanking, which ceded Hong Kong and opened five treaty ports; the Second (1856 to 1860) ended with the occupation of Beijing and the burning of the Old Summer Palace. China remembers them as the start of its century of humiliation.

steps.title: Lin Zexu and the opium crisis
steps.text: British merchants were smuggling vast amounts of Indian opium into China. The emperor sent Lin Zexu to Canton, where he forced the foreign merchants to hand over their stocks and destroyed over 1,000 tonnes of opium at Humen. The British superintendent Charles Elliot withdrew to the waters off Hong Kong, and clashes with Chinese war junks at Kowloon and Chuenpi began the war.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Destruction of opium at Humen
events.text: Lin Zexu had the seized opium mixed with lime and salt and washed into the sea.

events.name: First Battle of Chuenpi
events.text: Two British frigates beat a fleet of Chinese war junks at the mouth of the Pearl River.

steps.label: 1840 to 1841
steps.title: The British expedition
steps.text: A British fleet arrived from India in 1840, blockaded Canton, seized Zhoushan island and sailed north to the Peiho, frightening the court into talks. Elliot's Convention of Chuenpi ceded Hong Kong, but both governments rejected it; the British stormed the Bogue forts and attacked Canton, which paid a ransom to be spared.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: British fleet north to the Peiho
Attack up the Pearl River on Canton

events.name: Capture of Zhoushan
events.text: The British took Dinghai as a base near the Yangtze mouth.

events.name: Battle of the Bogue
events.text: British ships and troops destroyed the forts guarding the Pearl River.

events.name: Battle of Canton
events.text: With the city at their mercy the British accepted a ransom of six million dollars.

steps.label: 1841 to 1842
steps.title: Up the Yangtze to Nanking
steps.text: Henry Pottinger replaced Elliot and took the war north: Amoy, Ningbo and Zhapu fell, and a Qing counteroffensive at Ningbo failed. In 1842 the British fleet entered the Yangtze, stormed Zhenjiang and cut the Grand Canal, then anchored off Nanjing. The Treaty of Nanking ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports to trade and imposed a large indemnity.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: British offensive up the coast and the Yangtze

events.name: Battle of Chinkiang
events.text: Manchu bannermen fought to the death, but the city fell and the Grand Canal was cut.

events.name: Treaty of Nanking
events.text: China ceded Hong Kong and opened Canton, Amoy, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai.

steps.label: 1856 to 1857
steps.title: The Arrow War
steps.text: With China weakened by the Taiping Rebellion, Britain seized on the boarding of the ship Arrow at Canton to reopen the war, and France joined over the execution of a missionary. Lord Elgin and Baron Gros led an Anglo-French force that captured Canton in late 1857 and carried off its governor, Ye Mingchen.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Arrow incident
events.text: Chinese officers boarded a Hong Kong registered ship, giving Britain its pretext.

events.name: Capture of Canton
events.text: Anglo-French troops stormed the city and captured Ye Mingchen.

steps.label: 1858 to 1859
steps.title: Taku Forts and Tientsin
steps.text: The allied fleet sailed north, took the Taku Forts guarding the Peiho and reached Tianjin, where the Qing signed treaties opening more ports, the Yangtze and Beijing itself to foreign envoys. When the envoys returned in 1859 to ratify them, Sengge Rinchen's rebuilt forts beat off Admiral Hope's attack.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: Allied fleet to the Peiho and Tianjin

events.name: First Battle of Taku Forts
events.text: Allied gunboats silenced the forts and opened the river.

events.name: Treaty of Tientsin
events.text: China agreed to open ports, legations in Beijing and legal opium imports.

events.name: Second Battle of Taku Forts
events.text: Qing gunners sank several British gunboats and repulsed the landing.

steps.title: The march on Beijing
steps.text: Britain and France sent a large army under Hope Grant and Cousin-Montauban, which landed at Beitang, took the Taku Forts from the rear and advanced on Beijing. Sengge Rinchen's cavalry was destroyed at Baliqiao, the emperor fled, and after Chinese captors killed allied prisoners Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace burned. The Convention of Peking ratified the treaties and ceded Kowloon.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: British army from Beitang to Beijing
French army to the Summer Palace
Qing army falls back on Beijing

events.name: Third Battle of Taku Forts
events.text: The allies stormed the northern fort and the rest surrendered.

events.name: Battle of Baliqiao
events.text: Allied firepower destroyed Sengge Rinchen's Mongol cavalry outside Beijing.

events.name: Convention of Peking
events.text: China ratified the treaties and ceded Kowloon after the Old Summer Palace was burned.

name: French conquest of Algeria
summary: France invaded the Regency of Algiers in 1830, took the city in three weeks and then spent seventeen years conquering the interior. The emir Abd al-Qadir built an Algerian state and led a long resistance until Marshal Bugeaud's campaigns of devastation, a war with Morocco and the loss of his support forced his surrender in 1847. Algeria became France's largest colony, at a heavy cost in Algerian lives.

steps.title: The fall of Algiers
steps.text: Using an insult to the French consul as pretext, the government of Charles X sent a fleet and 34,000 troops under Bourmont. The army landed at Sidi Ferruch, beat the Dey's forces at Staoueli and forced Algiers to capitulate on 5 July 1830. Hussein Dey went into exile, and France found itself holding a coast whose interior it did not control.

events.name: Battle of Staoueli
events.text: French troops routed the Dey's army a few days after landing.

events.name: Capture of Algiers
events.text: The Dey surrendered the city and its treasury after the Fort l'Empereur was blown up.

steps.label: 1832 to 1837
steps.title: Abd al-Qadir and Constantine
steps.text: In the west the tribes chose the young Abd al-Qadir as emir, and he built a state and army around Mascara, routing a French column at La Macta in 1835. In the east Ahmed Bey held Constantine and threw back a first French assault in 1836. France then made peace with Abd al-Qadir at the Tafna, recognising his rule over two thirds of Algeria, and stormed Constantine in 1837.

moves.label: Emir's army against the Oran column

events.name: Battle of La Macta
events.text: Abd al-Qadir ambushed and routed General Trezel's column in the marshes.

events.name: Treaty of Tafna
events.text: France recognised Abd al-Qadir's authority over most of western and central Algeria.

events.name: Siege of Constantine
events.text: French troops stormed the rock city at the second attempt and ended Ahmed Bey's rule.

steps.label: 1839 to 1843
steps.title: Bugeaud's war of devastation
steps.text: Abd al-Qadir declared holy war again in 1839 after a French column crossed his territory, and his raiders devastated the Mitidja plain behind Algiers. Bugeaud, governor from 1841, answered with fast columns that burned crops and villages, and took the emir's fortress towns of Tagdempt and Mascara. In 1843 the Duke of Aumale captured the emir's mobile capital, the smala, at Taguin, and Abd al-Qadir fell back toward Morocco.

events.name: Capture of the smala
events.text: Aumale's cavalry seized the emir's tent city with thousands of followers.

events.name: Fall of Tagdempt and Mascara
events.text: Bugeaud destroyed the emir's fortified bases.

steps.title: War with Morocco
steps.text: When the Sultan of Morocco sheltered Abd al-Qadir, France went to war. Prince de Joinville's squadron bombarded Tangier and Mogador, and Bugeaud defeated a large Moroccan army under the Sultan's son at the Isly river near Oujda. The Treaty of Tangier forced Morocco to outlaw the emir.

moves.label: Bugeaud from Tlemcen to the Isly
Naval squadron along the Moroccan coast

events.name: Bombardment of Tangier
events.text: Joinville's ships destroyed the harbour defences.

events.name: Battle of Isly
events.text: Bugeaud's infantry squares broke the Moroccan cavalry.

events.name: Bombardment of Mogador
events.text: The French shelled the port and occupied the island off it.

steps.label: 1845 to 1847
steps.title: The last resistance
steps.text: A great revolt in the Dahra mountains under Bou Maza in 1845 was crushed with brutal methods, including the suffocation of villagers in caves. Abd al-Qadir returned from Morocco and wiped out a French column at Sidi Brahim, but Moroccan troops now hunted him too. Cornered, he surrendered to Lamoriciere in December 1847 and went into exile.

events.name: Battle of Sidi Brahim
events.text: Abd al-Qadir destroyed a French column of chasseurs.

events.name: Surrender of Abd al-Qadir
events.text: The emir gave himself up near Ghazaouet, ending organised resistance in the west.

name: Mexican–American War
summary: After the United States annexed Texas, a border dispute over the Rio Grande led to war with Mexico in 1846. American armies won in northern Mexico, seized New Mexico and California, and Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz and fought his way to Mexico City. In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Mexico ceded about half its territory, the future American Southwest, which deepened the American quarrel over slavery.

steps.label: Apr to May 1846
steps.title: War on the Rio Grande
steps.text: President Polk sent Zachary Taylor's army to the Rio Grande, into land Mexico considered its own. After Mexican cavalry ambushed an American patrol, Taylor beat Arista's larger army at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma and crossed into Matamoros, and Congress declared war.

moves.label: Army of Occupation to the Rio Grande
Mexican Army of the North crosses the river

events.name: Battle of Palo Alto
events.text: American artillery broke up Arista's attacks in the opening battle.

events.name: Battle of Resaca de la Palma
events.text: Taylor routed the Mexican army back across the Rio Grande.

steps.label: Jun 1846 to Jan 1847
steps.title: Monterrey, New Mexico and California
steps.text: Taylor pushed into northern Mexico and took Monterrey after three days of street fighting. Kearny's Army of the West marched from Fort Leavenworth, took Santa Fe without a fight and crossed the desert to California, where American settlers and naval forces had risen. By January 1847 the United States held New Mexico and California.

moves.commander: John C. Fremont and Robert F. Stockton
moves.label: Conquest of California

events.name: Battle of Monterrey
events.text: Ampudia surrendered the city to Taylor after fierce street fighting.

events.name: Occupation of Santa Fe
events.text: Kearny took New Mexico's capital without firing a shot.

events.name: Treaty of Cahuenga
events.text: Californio forces surrendered, ending the fighting in California.

steps.label: Feb 1847
steps.title: Buena Vista
steps.text: Santa Anna, back in power, marched north from San Luis Potosi to destroy Taylor's weakened army. In two days of fighting at Buena Vista near Saltillo the outnumbered Americans held their ground, and Santa Anna withdrew south. It was the last major battle in northern Mexico.

moves.label: Taylor to Agua Nueva and back to Buena Vista

events.name: Battle of Buena Vista
events.text: Taylor's army survived Santa Anna's assaults and the Mexican army retreated.

steps.label: Mar to Sep 1847
steps.title: Scott's march on Mexico City
steps.text: Winfield Scott made the largest amphibious landing yet seen at Veracruz and took the city after a siege. He beat Santa Anna in the mountain pass at Cerro Gordo, paused at Puebla, then fought his way into the Valley of Mexico. After the storming of Chapultepec castle the capital fell on 14 September 1847.

moves.label: Santa Anna falls back on the capital

events.name: Siege of Veracruz
events.text: The port surrendered after a heavy bombardment.

events.name: Battle of Cerro Gordo
events.text: Scott outflanked Santa Anna's fortified pass and opened the road inland.

events.name: Battle of Chapultepec
events.text: American troops stormed the castle and entered Mexico City the next day.

steps.title: Guadalupe Hidalgo
steps.text: With its capital occupied, Mexico signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in February 1848. It accepted the Rio Grande border and ceded California, New Mexico and the lands between for 15 million dollars, and the American army went home. Gold was found in California the same year.

events.name: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
events.text: Mexico ceded about 55 percent of its territory to the United States.

name: Hungarian Revolution and War of Independence
summary: In the revolutions of 1848 Hungary won self-government from the Habsburgs, and when Vienna moved to take it back the conflict became a war. Hungarian armies under Gorgei and Bem drove the Austrians out in the spring of 1849 and the Diet declared independence, but Russia sent some 200,000 troops to help Austria. Crushed between two empires, the Hungarian army surrendered at Vilagos in August 1849 and Austria imposed harsh reprisals.

steps.label: Mar to Oct 1848
steps.title: Revolution and the Croatian invasion
steps.text: On 15 March 1848 a revolution in Pest won the April Laws, giving Hungary its own government under the Habsburg crown, with Kossuth as finance minister. Vienna encouraged the Croatian ban Jelacic to invade, but Hungarian forces stopped him at Pakozd and he retreated toward Vienna. A Hungarian army that followed him was beaten at Schwechat, just as Windischgratz crushed the revolution in Vienna.

events.name: March Revolution in Pest
events.text: Students and the poet Petofi launched the revolution with the Twelve Points.

events.name: Battle of Pakozd
events.text: The new Hungarian army halted Jelacic's advance on Pest.

events.name: Battle of Schwechat
events.text: The Hungarians failed to relieve revolutionary Vienna.

steps.label: Dec 1848 to Feb 1849
steps.title: Windischgratz takes Buda-Pest
steps.text: Windischgratz invaded Hungary from the west and entered Buda-Pest in January 1849, while the Kossuth government fled to Debrecen behind the Tisza. Gorgei led his army on a winter retreat through the mountains of Upper Hungary, and in Transylvania the Polish general Bem began to drive out the Austrians.

moves.label: Gorgei's winter retreat through Upper Hungary

events.name: Fall of Buda-Pest
events.text: The Hungarian government abandoned the capital for Debrecen.

events.name: Battle of Kapolna
events.text: Windischgratz checked the Hungarian advance and wrongly reported the revolt crushed.

steps.label: Apr to May 1849
steps.title: The Spring Campaign
steps.text: Gorgei's reorganised armies struck west and beat the Austrians at Isaszeg and Nagysallo, relieving the fortress of Komarom and forcing them out of almost all of Hungary. On 14 April the Diet at Debrecen declared independence and made Kossuth governor-president, and in May the Hungarians stormed Buda Castle.

events.name: Battle of Isaszeg
events.text: Gorgei drove Windischgratz back on Pest.

events.name: Hungarian Declaration of Independence
events.text: The Diet dethroned the Habsburgs and made Kossuth head of state.

events.name: Siege of Buda
events.text: Hungarian troops stormed the castle after a three-week siege.

steps.label: Jun to Aug 1849
steps.title: Russian intervention and Vilagos
steps.text: Tsar Nicholas I sent Paskevich over the Carpathians with about 200,000 men, while Haynau's reinforced Austrian army advanced from the west and retook Buda-Pest. Russian troops crushed Bem at Segesvar, where the poet Petofi died, and Haynau beat the main Hungarian army at Temesvar. Gorgei surrendered to the Russians at Vilagos on 13 August; thirteen of his generals were executed at Arad.

moves.label: Russian main army over the Dukla Pass

events.name: Battle of Segesvar
events.text: Luders routed Bem's army; Sandor Petofi was killed.

events.name: Battle of Temesvar
events.text: Haynau defeated the main southern Hungarian army under Bem.

events.name: Surrender at Vilagos
events.text: Gorgei laid down arms before the Russians, ending the war.

name: Crimean War
summary: Russia's pressure on the Ottoman Empire over the Danubian Principalities and the protection of Orthodox Christians brought war in 1853, and Britain and France joined the Ottomans in 1854 to stop Russian expansion. The allies landed in Crimea and besieged the naval base of Sevastopol for almost a year, at terrible cost from disease and incompetence on all sides. The Treaty of Paris neutralised the Black Sea and checked Russia, which turned to reform after its defeat.

sides.name: Ottoman Empire, France, Britain and Sardinia

steps.label: Jul to Nov 1853
steps.title: Russia moves on the Danube
steps.text: Tsar Nicholas I sent his army into the Ottoman vassal principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia in July 1853. The Ottomans declared war, and Omar Pasha's troops held the Danube and won at Oltenita. Then the Russian Black Sea Fleet under Nakhimov annihilated an Ottoman squadron at Sinop, which inflamed British and French opinion.

events.name: Battle of Oltenita
events.text: Omar Pasha's troops repulsed a Russian attack on their Danube bridgehead.

events.name: Battle of Sinop
events.text: Russian shell-firing ships destroyed the Ottoman squadron in harbour.

steps.title: The allies land in Crimea
steps.text: Britain and France declared war in March 1854. The Ottomans held Silistra, and under Austrian pressure Russia withdrew from the principalities, so the allies sailed from Varna to destroy the naval base at Sevastopol. They beat Menshikov at the Alma, survived Russian attacks at Balaklava, where the Light Brigade charged, and at Inkerman, then settled into a winter siege.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: Allied expedition from Varna to Crimea

events.name: Siege of Silistra
events.text: The Ottoman garrison held out and the Russians abandoned the siege.

events.name: Battle of the Alma
events.text: Allied troops stormed the heights above the river and opened the road to Sevastopol.

events.name: Battle of Balaklava
events.text: The Russians failed to take the British base, remembered for the Charge of the Light Brigade.

steps.title: The fall of Sevastopol
steps.text: The siege dragged on through a winter of cold, cholera and scandal, until Florence Nightingale's reforms and a new railway eased the British army's suffering. Sardinia sent an army, the allies beat a Russian relief attempt on the Chernaya, and on 8 September the French under MacMahon stormed the Malakoff, forcing the Russians to abandon Sevastopol. In the Caucasus Muravyov starved Kars into surrender.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

moves.label: Russian relief army on the Chernaya

events.name: Battle of the Chernaya
events.text: French and Sardinian troops threw back the last Russian attempt to break the siege.

events.name: Storming of the Malakoff
events.text: The French took the key fortification and the Russians evacuated Sevastopol.

events.name: Siege of Kars
events.text: The starving Ottoman garrison surrendered, giving Russia a bargaining chip.

steps.title: The Peace of Paris
steps.text: Exhausted, Russia accepted peace after Austria threatened to join the allies. The Treaty of Paris in March 1856 returned Kars and Sevastopol, demilitarised the Black Sea and put the principalities under joint European guarantee. Russia's defeat pushed Tsar Alexander II toward the emancipation of the serfs.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Treaty of Paris
events.text: The Black Sea was neutralised and Russia lost southern Bessarabia.
